title: Genesis and Growth of Nehruism, Vol. 1: Commitment to Communism
byline: by Sita Ram Goel · first published as eighteen articles by “Ekaki” in the Organiser, June–October 1961 · Voice of India edition 1993, with a foreword by Philip Spratt
lede: In 1961, with Krishna Menon as Defence Minister and China pressing on the Himalayan frontier, Goel set out to show from Nehru's own words that he was neither neutral nor a democratic socialist but a lifelong “fellow-traveller” of Soviet Communism. He builds his case almost entirely from quotations: five of Nehru's books, his speeches as Prime Minister and his foreign policy. The foreword is by Philip Spratt, a former British Communist organiser in India who had turned anti-Communist.
facts: weekly articles in 1961, plus a 1962 essay and a 1993 postscript
Nehru books examined, from Soviet Russia (1929) to The Discovery of India (1946)
Nehru's first visit to Moscow, the root of the story in Goel's telling
Panchsheel signed. Goel says Chinese incursions began almost at once and were kept secret.
note: This is a Cold War polemic, and its portrait of Nehru is deliberately one-sided. As a reader complains in chapter 12, it collects only the “yes” quotations. Historians generally see Nehru as a non-aligned democratic socialist. This page reports Goel's case as his.
